Actions on Objectives
Likely
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] SonicWall SMA1000 SSRF exploitation via /wsproxy endpoint (CVE-2026-15409) · [LLM] SonicWall SMA1000 command injection via sysCtrl.execRemoveHotfix RPC (CVE-2026-15410) · Article-specific behavioural hunt — SonicWall SMA1000 flaws exploited as zero-days to push custom malware
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] KNUCKLEBALL dropper and Sou5/ORANGETAIL/ROOTRUN malware artifacts on SMA1000 · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] UTA0533 SonicWall SMA C2 / infrastructure IP communication · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
SonicWall SMA1000 SSRF exploitation via /wsproxy endpoint (CVE-2026-15409) AIExploitation High
Hunts unauthenticated WebSocket-tunnel abuse of the SMA1000 '/wsproxy' endpoint that UTA0533 used to reach internal-only services (CouchDB, management RPC) during the first stage of the exploit chain. Article-specific because it anchors on the exact endpoint path Volexity attributed to CVE-2026-15409. Rationale: Anchors on the verbatim '/wsproxy' endpoint (code block 1) that Volexity tied to CVE-2026-15409 SSRF; requests to this path from external sources are not part of normal SMA1000 client traffic. Cross-checked against: • https://www.volexity.com/blog/ • https://psirt.sonicwall.com/
ATT&CKT1190 T1090
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • SonicWall support engineer running diagnostics against the appliance web UI
  • Internal vulnerability scanner (Nessus/Qualys) crawling the SMA1000 URI space
  • Legitimate WebSocket VPN client sessions that also traverse a proxy path prefix
  • Load-balancer/uptime health-check hitting appliance paths
  • Penetration-test engagement replaying the disclosed PoC
Suppression filter
| where SourceIP !in ("<known-scanner-ips>")   // maintain org scanner allowlist as a watchlist join instead of inline
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): pull all CommonSecurityLog rows for the SMA1000 with RequestURL containing /wsproxy; note SourceIP, correlate against the UTA0533 IP list and confirm whether the source is external/unauthenticated. Step 2 (contain): if source is untrusted, block the IP at the perimeter firewall, isolate the appliance from internal segments (CouchDB/mgmt), and confirm it is patched to 12.4.3-03453 / 12.5.0-02835. Step 3 (hunt): pivot on the same SourceIP for follow-on sysCtrl.execRemoveHotfix RPC calls, product_uuid queries, and outbound connections to UTA0533 C2 IPs.
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DeviceVendor has "SonicWall" or DeviceProduct has_any ("SMA", "Secure Mobile Access")
| where RequestURL has "/wsproxy"
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, SourceIP, DestinationIP, DestinationPort, RequestMethod, RequestURL, DeviceAction
| order by TimeGenerated desc

    cs-uri-stem|contains: '/wsproxy'
  condition: selection

| tstats summariesonly=true count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Web where Web.url="*/wsproxy*" by Web.src Web.dest Web.dest_port Web.http_method Web.url Web.status | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)` | sort - lastTime
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Web where Web.url="*/wsproxy*" by Web.src Web.dest Web.dest_port Web.http_method Web.url Web.status | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)` | sort - lastTime
SonicWall SMA1000 command injection via sysCtrl.execRemoveHotfix RPC (CVE-2026-15410) AIExploitation High
Hunts invocation of the Appliance Management Console 'sysCtrl.execRemoveHotfix' RPC method that UTA0533 abused for CVE-2026-15410 command injection to gain root on SMA1000 appliances. Article-specific because it keys on the exact RPC method name Volexity documented for stage two. Rationale: Anchors on the verbatim 'sysCtrl.execRemoveHotfix' RPC method (code block 3) that Volexity attributed to CVE-2026-15410 command injection; this management RPC has no legitimate remote-attacker context and is rare in normal appliance operation. Cross-checked against: • https://www.volexity.com/blog/ • https://psirt.sonicwall.com/
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.004
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • SonicWall administrator legitimately removing a hotfix during patch rollback
  • Vendor support session performing appliance maintenance
  • Automated appliance orchestration/config-management removing hotfixes
  • Log replay during forensic reconstruction of the incident
  • Firmware upgrade workflow that internally calls the same RPC
Suppression filter
| where SyslogMessage !has "scheduled-maintenance" and Computer in ("<sma1000-appliance-hostnames>")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): review the SyslogMessage around each execRemoveHotfix call for injected shell metacharacters / unexpected command strings and confirm which console session (source IP / admin) invoked it. Step 2 (contain): if the caller is unauthenticated or matches UTA0533 infrastructure, isolate the appliance, rotate appliance admin credentials and product_uuid-derived secrets, and verify the 12.4.3-03453 / 12.5.0-02835 patch level. Step 3 (hunt): search the same appliance for KNUCKLEBALL 'deploy_new.py', Sou5 'agent_wp8.jar', ORANGETAIL 'agent_wp9.jar', ROOTRUN artifacts, and nginx config modifications exposing the webshell.
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where SyslogMessage has "sysCtrl.execRemoveHotfix" or SyslogMessage has "execRemoveHotfix"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, HostIP, ProcessName, Facility, SeverityLevel, SyslogMessage
| order by TimeGenerated desc
source:linux.syslog execRemoveHotfix
APPLICATION
search (sourcetype=sonicwall OR sourcetype=syslog) "sysCtrl.execRemoveHotfix" | stats count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(host) as appliance by _raw | sort - lastTime
UTA0533 SonicWall SMA C2 / infrastructure IP communication AICommand & Control Medium
Detects any inbound or outbound network communication with the eight UTA0533 infrastructure IPs Volexity published for the SonicWall SMA1000 campaign, covering exploitation source IPs and Sou5 reverse-proxy / ORANGETAIL webshell C2. Article-specific because it uses the exact confirmed IOC IP set. Rationale: Uses the exact eight campaign IPs from the article's pre-extracted IOC set; dedicated attacker infrastructure means any hit is high-fidelity regardless of direction. Cross-checked against: • https://www.volexity.com/blog/ • https://psirt.sonicwall.com/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1090
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • An IP is later reassigned to a benign hoster and reused by legitimate services (validate against IOC expiration/last-seen dates)
  • Threat-intel platform or sandbox detonating samples that beacon to these IPs
  • Security researcher scanning the attacker infrastructure from a corporate host
  • Shared VPS provider IP where only a virtual host was malicious
  • Passive DNS / scanning appliance touching the IPs during enrichment
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("sandboxagent.exe", "cuckoo.exe")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): identify the internal host/appliance on the other side of the connection, connection direction, port, and byte volume; confirm the IOC IP is still active per current threat intel. Step 2 (contain): block the IP bidirectionally at the firewall, isolate the involved host/SMA1000 appliance, and capture memory/disk before reboot. Step 3 (hunt): pivot on the internal host for KNUCKLEBALL/Sou5/ORANGETAIL file artifacts, /wsproxy and execRemoveHotfix log entries, and any lateral movement from the compromised appliance into internal subnets.

KNUCKLEBALL dropper and Sou5/ORANGETAIL/ROOTRUN malware artifacts on SMA1000 AIInstallation Medium
Retro-hunts the UTA0533 custom SonicWall SMA1000 tooling by exact filename (deploy_new.py, agent_wp8.jar, agent_wp9.jar) and Volexity-published file hashes across endpoint/EDR telemetry and forwarded appliance file events. Article-specific because it targets the named malware families and their confirmed hashes, not a generic dropped-file heuristic. Rationale: Anchors on the named custom malware files (deploy_new.py, agent_wp8.jar, agent_wp9.jar) and the four Volexity SHA256 hashes from the article's IOC set; these are bespoke SMA1000 tooling with no legitimate presence. Cross-checked against: • https://www.volexity.com/blog/ • https://psirt.sonicwall.com/
ATT&CKT1105 T1505.003 T1068
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Incident-response analyst copying captured samples onto a forensic workstation for analysis
  • Malware sample stored in a threat-intel/sandbox repository host
  • Backup/restore job moving a compromised appliance image containing the artifacts
  • AV quarantine relocating the files (matches hash but is benign remediation)
  • Generic filename collision on agent_wp8.jar in an unrelated Java app (hash check disambiguates)
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("7z.exe", "explorer.exe", "mpcmdrun.exe") and FolderPath !has "\\Quarantine\\"
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): confirm the hit is a live drop vs. analyst/forensic handling by checking the writing process, host role, and whether SHA256 matches the Volexity IOCs. Step 2 (contain): isolate the host/appliance, preserve the KNUCKLEBALL dropper and jars for analysis, and rotate any credentials/secrets accessible from the SMA1000. Step 3 (hunt): on confirmed hosts, look for the nginx config modification exposing ORANGETAIL, ROOTRUN privilege-escalation execution, product_uuid/CouchDB access, and outbound connections to the UTA0533 C2 IP set.

Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s) Reconnaissance High

ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-15409", "CVE-2026-15410")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-15409", "CVE-2026-15410")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["81a9af3846bad3a1107164ff7cf0a08e020b31a3b32fd17866e17d4c1565f7f2", "8c470301dcb7278f73e622f1950073567b34011c64b60cdfbb0f89803923a5a3", "1e1e68bbb899450a57274a8b12082ed4e2040a2aae77014f20431689d2b4edee", "ea9154e374e4f77bc2cf54282e23543573980342a85bc888cb23f20b8bbba081", "04d4a9fbb32e967200eb98be014ca914a03bfa6b", "b4ee1f50fbb49f0ff5fde3d026343bc23ee08d51", "c2b0ae0a1f42a139abe4dd612676066ec1426394", "5e5b716f2385c818ec61198be1a2a07a4560eac5", "5cb00bbfe818ee3e85fb99ab1db1af7c", "b6df166291f80ee89032d769c99714f3", "54d21399b8b52b48a0fef68450593e45", "5f3a55201c511c9ff9be4c16c41028a2"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Vulnerable node-tar (<=7.5.18) present on hosts — CVE-2026-59873 decompression-bomb DoS exposure AIWeaponization High
Surfaces every host where Defender/vuln-scanner telemetry reports the npm 'tar' package at or below 7.5.18, the range vulnerable to CVE-2026-59873 (unbounded decompressed-data DoS / Gzip bomb). This is the attack-surface inventory pivot: any service extracting untrusted archives with this version can be forced to exhaust disk/CPU with a tiny crafted input. Fixed in 7.5.19. Rationale: Pivots on the exact CVE id and the concrete affected range from the advisory (npm 'tar' <= 7.5.18, fixed 7.5.19). CVE-id equality in TVM/scanner data is a high-fidelity exposure list with near-zero FP — the only 'noise' is remediated-but-not-rescanned hosts. Cross-checked against: • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-59874 • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-23hp-3jrh-7fpw • https://www.tenable.com/cve/CVE-2026-59874 • https://github.com/isaacs/node-tar/security
ATT&CKT1499.004
Data sourcesVulnerabilities.Vulnerabilities
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Host patched to 7.5.19+ but not yet re-scanned, so TVM snapshot is stale
  • 'tar' package pinned inside a container image layer that never extracts untrusted input (internal build tarballs only)
  • Nested/transitive copy of tar in node_modules of a dev-only dependency not reachable at runtime
  • Scanner fingerprints a vendored copy of tar sources without a functioning install
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the flagged host actually runs a service that extracts attacker-supplied archives (npm registry mirror, CI/CD artifact unpack, file-upload/import feature) — internal-only tarball handling is lower priority. 2) Contain: schedule `npm i tar@7.5.19` (or bump the transitive pin via overrides/resolutions) on internet-facing extractors first; add a temporary reverse-proxy body-size cap on upload endpoints. 3) Hunt: pull last 7d of file-write telemetry for the host's node processes and run UC2 to check whether a decompression bomb was already attempted.

node.js process rapidly writing multi-GB file during archive extraction (CVE-2026-59873 gzip-bomb impact) AIActions on Objectives Low
Hunts the runtime signature of the node-tar decompression bomb: a node process extracting an archive and writing an abnormally large single file (multi-GB) from a tiny compressed input, driving toward disk exhaustion. Article-specific because the vuln has no total-bytes/entry-count guard, so extraction writes far more data than the input warrants. Rationale: Targets the article's core impact — node-tar writes gigabytes to disk from a negligible compressed stream because there is no cumulative-bytes limit. Pivots on node as the initiating process plus an anomalous single-file size / write-volume, the observable footprint of the Gzip bomb described in the PoC. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-23hp-3jrh-7fpw • https://github.com/isaacs/node-tar/security
ATT&CKT1499.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: high — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate large-artifact extraction in CI (multi-GB container layers, ML model tarballs, dataset archives)
  • Node-based backup/restore or migration jobs that genuinely unpack large archives
  • Log-rotation or cache builds where a node service writes a large single file
  • Package-mirror sync (e.g. Verdaccio/nexus) unpacking large legitimate packages
  • Electron/build tooling emitting a large bundled asset
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("backup","restore","webpack","electron-builder","model","dataset") or FolderPath has_any ("\\ci\\","\\build\\","\\artifacts\\","/ci/","/build/","/artifacts/"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: check the InitiatingProcessCommandLine and FolderPath — is this a known CI/build/backup job writing to an expected artifact path, or an internet-facing upload/import service writing to a temp/extraction dir? Correlate the host against UC1 (is tar<=7.5.18 present?). 2) Contain: if unexplained, kill the node PID and quarantine the source archive; add disk-quota/ulimit on the extraction directory and a body-size limit on the upload endpoint. 3) Hunt: search the same host+window for the inbound tiny archive (small POST/upload immediately preceding the write burst) and for repeated attempts across other extractor hosts.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","node")
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
| summarize MaxFileSize = max(FileSize), Writes = count(), FirstWrite = min(Timestamp), LastWrite = max(Timestamp) by DeviceName, FolderPath, FileName, InitiatingProcessId, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| where MaxFileSize > 2147483648   // >2GB single file from a node extraction; gzip-bomb hallmark vs tiny input
| extend WriteWindowSec = datetime_diff('second', LastWrite, FirstWrite)
| order by MaxFileSize desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActingProcessName has "node"
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
| summarize MaxFileSize = max(TargetFileSize), Writes = count(), FirstWrite = min(TimeGenerated), LastWrite = max(TimeGenerated) by DvcHostname, TargetFilePath, ActingProcessId, ActingProcessCommandLine
| where MaxFileSize > 2147483648   // >2GB single file written by node during extraction
| extend WriteWindowSec = datetime_diff('second', LastWrite, FirstWrite)
| order by MaxFileSize desc
#event_simpleName=FileWritten ContextImageFileName=/node(\.exe)?$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, TargetFileName], function=sum(WrittenBytes, as=TotalBytes))
| TotalBytes > 2147483648

LightRAG destructive document ops post-bypass (DELETE /documents, clear_cache, unauth upload) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the impact stage of CVE-2026-61740 exploitation: destructive or ingestion calls to the LightRAG document API — DELETE /documents (wipes the corpus), /documents/clear_cache (destroys LLM/embedding caches) and /documents/upload|scan|file_batch (attacker-controlled ingestion). These are inherently rare, high-consequence operations that map directly to the advisory's confidentiality/integrity/availability impact. Rationale: Uses the exact destructive LightRAG endpoints named in the advisory impact section — DELETE /documents, /documents/clear_cache, /documents/upload|scan|file_batch|texts — which are rare, high-consequence operations. The DELETE-against-/documents shape is the corpus-wipe primitive the PoC demonstrated returning HTTP 200. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-f4vv-55c2-5789 • https://cve.threatint.eu/CVE/CVE-2026-61740
ATT&CKT1485 T1496 T1190
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Administrator performing a legitimate corpus refresh (bulk /documents/upload or /documents/scan) during scheduled re-ingestion
  • Operational runbook clearing caches via /documents/clear_cache after a model/embedding change
  • A data pipeline that deletes and reloads the knowledge base on a schedule (DELETE /documents followed by re-upload)
  • CI / staging environments exercising the document API during automated tests
  • Backup/migration tooling snapshotting then clearing the document store
Suppression filter
| where RequestMethod =~ "DELETE"   // narrow to the pure corpus-destruction primitive, dropping benign upload/scan/cache-clear ingestion noise
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Identify the SourceIP and RequestMethod/RequestURL; confirm whether the call carried an X-API-Key (legitimate ops) or was preceded by a Bearer guest-JWT request (UC1) from the same IP — the latter confirms CVE-2026-61740 abuse. Check whether a change window/runbook explains it. 2) CONTAIN: Block the SourceIP, take the LightRAG instance off the public interface, and upgrade to lightrag-hku >=1.5.4; rotate TOKEN_SECRET and LIGHTRAG_API_KEY. 3) HUNT: Enumerate every document/graph/query call from that IP to quantify what was read, deleted, ingested (potential poisoning) or queried (LLM-credit exhaustion), and diff the current document store against the last backup to assess destruction.

LightRAG CVE-2026-61736: cross-origin credentialed read of /documents or /query (data exfil) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts credentialed cross-origin HTTP requests to LightRAG's sensitive API endpoints (/documents, /query, /query/data) where the Referer/Origin host differs from the LightRAG host — the exploitation signature of the CORS wildcard + allow_credentials flaw. A malicious site the victim visits rides their authenticated session to exfiltrate documents and knowledge-graph data. Rationale: Anchored on LightRAG's article-named endpoints (/login, /documents) plus /query corroborated by the official API docs, combined with the CORS root cause: the exploit necessarily produces a credentialed request whose Referer/Origin host != the LightRAG host. Comparing referer-host to target-host is the highest-fidelity behavioural signal the flaw leaves in access logs. Cross-checked against: • https://www.thehackerwire.com/lightrag-critical-credentialed-cors-vulnerability/ • https://github.com/HKUDS/LightRAG/blob/main/docs/LightRAG-API-Server.md • https://cve.threatint.eu/CVE/CVE-2026-61736
ATT&CKT1185 T1213
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Split frontend/backend deployment where the LightRAG SPA is served from a different host/subdomain than the API, so legitimate reads carry a cross-origin Referer
  • API gateway or reverse proxy that rewrites Host, making Referer host legitimately differ from the logged CsHost
  • Grafana/BI dashboards or internal wikis embedding LightRAG query results with their own Referer
  • Swagger UI / ReDoc API console hosted on a separate documentation host
  • DAST scanners (Burp, OWASP ZAP) issuing requests with crafted Referer values
Suppression filter
| extend RefDomain = strcat_array(array_slice(split(RefererHost,"."), -2, -1), ".") | extend TgtDomain = strcat_array(array_slice(split(TargetHost,"."), -2, -1), ".") | where RefDomain != TgtDomain
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the offending RefererHost and CIp; confirm it is NOT a sanctioned internal frontend/gateway for this LightRAG instance and check whether the CsUsername session was concurrently active from a normal client. 2) Contain: set CORS_ORIGINS to an explicit allow-list (or allow_credentials=False) and upgrade lightrag-hku to >=1.5.4; if the RefererHost is an unknown external domain, block it at the proxy/WAF and force-invalidate active LightRAG tokens. 3) Hunt: sweep all LightRAG access logs for the same RefererHost across /documents, /query, /query/data and DELETE /documents; review volume of documents/knowledge-graph rows read to scope data exposure.
AppServiceHTTPLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where CsUriStem has_any ("/documents", "/query")
| where CsMethod in ("GET","POST")
| where isnotempty(Referer) and Referer != "-"
| extend RefererHost = tolower(tostring(parse_url(Referer).Host))
| extend TargetHost = tolower(tostring(split(CsHost, ":")[0]))
| where isnotempty(RefererHost) and RefererHost != TargetHost
| where RefererHost !in ("localhost", "127.0.0.1")
| project TimeGenerated, CsHost, CIp, CsUsername, CsMethod, CsUriStem, Referer, RefererHost, UserAgent, ScStatus
| order by TimeGenerated desc

LightRAG CVE-2026-61736: cross-origin DELETE of document store (destructive CORS abuse) AIActions on Objectives High
Alerts on a credentialed cross-origin DELETE against LightRAG's /documents endpoints where the Referer/Origin host differs from the LightRAG host. The advisory calls out 'deleting the entire document store' as a destructive impact of the wildcard-CORS-with-credentials flaw; a DELETE riding the victim's session from an external origin is high-fidelity data destruction. Rationale: Uses the article's explicitly stated destructive impact (delete the document store) mapped to LightRAG's real DELETE /documents and DELETE /documents/delete_document endpoints (confirmed in the API-server docs), qualified by the cross-origin Referer signature that only the CORS flaw produces — a very low-FP, high-severity combination. Cross-checked against: • https://www.thehackerwire.com/lightrag-critical-credentialed-cors-vulnerability/ • https://github.com/HKUDS/LightRAG/blob/main/docs/LightRAG-API-Server.md • https://cve.threatint.eu/CVE/CVE-2026-61736
ATT&CKT1485 T1185
Data sourcesWeb.Web

    where Vulnerabilities.signature IN ("CVE-2025-3248")
    by Vulnerabilities.dest, Vulnerabilities.signature, Vulnerabilities.severity, Vulnerabilities.cve
| `drop_dm_object_name(Vulnerabilities)`
| sort - severity
Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files

LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: LSASS Process Access Outside Microsoft-Signed Tooling
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d04
status: experimental
description: |
    Anything opening lsass.exe with read-memory access that isn't a
    Microsoft signed component (Defender, csrss, etc.) is suspect.
    Mimikatz / Pypykatz / nanodump signature.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1003/001/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:

    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: process_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection:
        TargetImage|endswith: '\lsass.exe'
    filter_known_good:

            - '\MsMpEng.exe'
            - '\csrss.exe'
            - '\svchost.exe'

            - '\services.exe'

Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement Actions on Objectives High
psexec / paexec / smbexec / wmic /node — service install over SMB from remote host.
ATT&CKT1021.002 T1569.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("psexec.exe","psexesvc.exe","paexec.exe","smbexec.py")
   or (FileName =~ "wmic.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has "/node:")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by Timestamp desc

SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688            // process-create (audit-policy required)
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\psexec.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\psexesvc.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\paexec.exe"
   or (NewProcessName endswith "\wmic.exe" and CommandLine has "/node:")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: PsExec / SMB Lateral Movement Tooling Execution
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d03
status: experimental
description: |
    PsExec, paexec, smbexec, csexec, remcom — admin-grade tooling that
    pivots over SMB. Pair with `wmic /node:` for the full cluster.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1021/002/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1569/002/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:

    - attack.t1569.002
    - attack.lateral-movement
